In a 1975 report, the Philadelphia City Planning Commission stated, "Philadelphia must deal with several important national and regional trends if it is to maintain its economic viability. First it must counteract the large scale migration of firms to the suburbs and other regions of the country. This migration has been led by manufacturing and trade firms whose jobs are particularly important to the city's residents."10/
Richmond, Virginia was one of eighteen cities included in the representation to this proceeding by the Short Haul Survival Committee and 252 Individual Motor Carriers. The Richmond Regional Planning District Commission pointed out in a May 1973 report that during the 1960's two of the counties bordering Richmond together accounted for over 80 percent of the region's increased population. The dispersion of commercial development in the Richmond region has followed population movements and the creation of suburban retail markets. Employment and new commercial/industrial growth from 1960-1972 has occurred primarily in areas outside the central city. 11/
~
The Continental Bank of Chicago has noted a recent trend toward relocation of truck terminals from Chicago's central business district to the suburbs. The bank survey of 100 terminal managers predicted the trend should continue at least through the 1980's. 12/
Although information presented above illustrates the trends toward decentralization and sprawl, it does not reveal how far commercial/industrial activities extend beyond municipal limits. The following discussion relates to that question.
Commercial/industrial locations and activities are generators of freight transportation and distribution. Their locations inside and outside municipalities indicate the geographical extent of decentralization and sprawl.
Commercial zone/terminal area boundaries which have been specifically defined by the Commission for certain cities are indicative of the decentralization of commerce/industry/institutions for those cities.
